title: Power budget
tagline: The reactor can't light every room. Decide who gets light.
briefing: The lights work, but the reactor is old. It runs in a cycle: a stretch at **full output** (6 lights), then a **cooling** stretch when it can only carry **3**. Ask for more lights than it can carry and the breaker trips: every light on the ship goes out.

So the ship no longer asks room by room. Once a tick it calls `planPower(rooms, supply)` with **all** the rooms at once and how many lights it can carry, and lights exactly the rooms whose names you return.
Your `lightOn` rule from level 1 is still in the file. You'll use it.
starter: // Your lighting rule from level 1. It still decides whether a room *wants* light.
// The reactor asks once a tick for the whole plan.
// rooms:  every room, like [{ name: "Engine", crew: 1, emergency: false }, ...]
// supply: how many lights the reactor can carry right now (6, or 3 while cooling)
// Return an array with the names of the rooms to light.

steps.title: Ask every room
text: The plan starts as an empty **array**, `[]`, so the whole ship is dark. An array is a list of values in order. `rooms` is an array too: six room objects.
A `for...of` loop runs its body once for each item in an array: `for (const room of rooms) { ... }` sets `room` to the first room, runs the body, then the second, and so on.
Inside, ask your old function: if `lightOn(room)` says yes, add the room's name to the plan with `plan.push(room.name)`. `push` adds an item to the end of an array.

predict.question: `rooms` holds six rooms. How many times does the loop's body run each tick?
predict.explain: A `for...of` loop visits every item, so the body runs six times, once per room. Now let it run until the log says the reactor is cooling, and watch the **Breaker trips** gauge.

goal.text: Every room that wants light is in the plan (at full power).

cases.label: Quiet ship
cases.why: lightOn says yes to Engine and Quarters (crew) and the Bridge (always).

hints: Start the loop with `for (const room of rooms) {` and end it with `}`, between `const plan = [];` and `return plan;`.

steps.title: Stay within the supply
text: When the reactor cools, `supply` drops to 3, but your plan still asks for every room that wants light. Ask for more than `supply` and the breaker trips. That's worse than lighting too few: then nothing is lit.
`plan.length` is how many names are in the plan so far. Only add a room while `plan.length < supply`.
You need **both** things to be true: the room wants light, **and** there's supply left. `&&` means *and*: `a && b` is `true` only if both sides are.

predict.question: `supply` is 3 and the plan already holds 3 names. What is `plan.length < supply`?
predict.explain: `3 < 3` is `false`: the plan is full, so no more names go in. If you wrote `<=` instead, a fourth name would get in and trip the breaker.

goal.text: The plan never asks for more lights than the supply.

cases.label: Cooling, busy ship
cases.why: Five rooms want light but the supply is 3: the first three in the list get it.

cases.label: Quiet ship, full power
cases.why: Plenty of supply: same as before.

hints: The change is in the `if` line inside the loop.

steps.title: Emergencies first
text: The breaker holds now. But watch a cooling cycle with an alarm in the Med bay or on the Bridge (the **Dark alarms** gauge): the rooms at the *start* of the list use up the supply, and an alarm near the end stays dark.
The order of the loop decides who gets light. So loop **twice**: the first loop adds only the emergency rooms; the second adds the others that want light.
`!` means *not*: it turns `true` into `false` and back. `!room.emergency` is true for a room *without* an emergency.

predict.question: In the second loop, what would go wrong without `!room.emergency`?
options: Emergency rooms would be added to the plan twice
predict.explain: `lightOn` says yes to every emergency room, so the second loop would push its name again. A name twice in the plan uses two lights for one room.

goal.text: Alarm rooms are lit before anything else, and no room is in the plan twice.

cases.label: Cooling, alarm at the end of the list
cases.why: The Med bay alarm is lit first; the two remaining lights go to the first rooms that want light.

cases.label: Full power, alarm in an empty room
cases.why: Plenty of supply: the alarm room, the crewed room and the Bridge. Each name once.

hints: Keep your loop, and add a new loop *above* it that only looks at emergencies.
The new loop's condition: `room.emergency && plan.length < supply`.
In the old loop, add `!room.emergency &&` at the start of the condition.

steps.title: Then the Bridge
text: Alarms are safe. But during cooling the Bridge, last in the list, still loses out to the crewed rooms, and the **Course** gauge sinks. Navigation matters more than reading lights.

Add a middle loop for the Bridge, between the alarms and everyone else. Then the last loop needs to skip *anything already in the plan*, not just emergencies. `plan.includes(name)` is `true` if that name is already in the array.
Three loops that look nearly alike is a sign. In Season 1 you'll learn to **sort** by priority instead; for now, the order of the loops *is* the priority.

predict.question: Why does the last loop check `!plan.includes(room.name)` instead of `!room.emergency`?
options: It also skips the Bridge, which the middle loop may already have added
predict.explain: `!room.emergency` only skips alarm rooms. The Bridge isn't an alarm room, so it would be added a second time. `!plan.includes(...)` skips *every* room already planned, whatever put it there.

goal.text: Priority: alarms, then the Bridge, then rooms with crew. Never a name twice.

cases.label: Cooling, everyone busy
cases.why: Alarm first, then the Bridge, then the first room with crew.

cases.label: Cooling, alarm on the Bridge
cases.why: The alarm already put the Bridge in the plan; it mustn't be added twice.

hints: You need three loops: alarms, the Bridge, everyone else.
The middle loop's condition: `room.name === "Bridge" && !plan.includes(room.name) && plan.length < supply`.
In the last loop, replace `!room.emergency` with `!plan.includes(room.name)`.

check.text: The reactor runs full and cooling cycles with alarms you haven't seen. Every plan must light the right rooms, in priority order, within the supply.

cases.label: Full power, quiet ship
cases.why: Everyone who needs light gets it, plus the Bridge.

cases.label: Cooling, crowded ship
cases.why: The Bridge first (navigation), then the first two crewed rooms.

cases.label: Cooling, alarm at the end of the list
Cooling, two alarms
cases.why: Both alarms, then the Bridge. Quarters waits for full power.

cases.label: Cooling, alarm on the Bridge
cases.why: The Bridge is in the plan once, not twice.

cases.label: Full power, everyone everywhere
cases.why: Six rooms want light and the supply is six.

cases.label: Supply of one, alarm in Cargo
cases.why: One light: the alarm wins, even over the Bridge.

solution: // Your lighting rule from level 1. It still decides whether a room *wants* light.
